extracted.intended_audience: general news readers interested in entertainment, comedy, and celebrity scandals
extracted.subtask_description: Writing or performing stand-up comedy that aims to expose wrongdoing or hypocrisy and shift public conversation; focuses on techniques and outcomes that make a routine socially consequential. Uses one comedian's 2014 routine about Bill Cosby as the exemplar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose hypocrisy by juxtaposing public persona and alleged behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Buress 'mocks Cosby's public scolding of the black community for bad behavior, alleging that Cosby has some shortcomings of his own.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrast between a subject's public moralizing and reported private misconduct to highlight hypocrisy. Technique often involves quoting or imitating the subject's own rhetoric and then undercutting it with factual or accusatory counterpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct, blunt accusation as a punchline
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted line: 'Yeah, but you raped women, Bill Cosby.' — delivered bluntly as part of the routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A straightforward, unambiguous accusation can deliver strong moral and comedic impact; risks include backlash, legal/ethical considerations, and personal attacks on the performer. Brevity and clarity increase shareability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of impersonation followed by the performer's own voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Buress impersonates Cosby ('Pull your pants up, black people. I was on TV in the ’80s...') then replies in his own voice with the accusation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switching from impersonation to the performer's voice emphasizes contrast and creates dramatic irony. Effective for satirizing a figure while making the commentator's stance unmistakable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call-to-action prompting audience to investigate
rubrics_metrics.description: Buress encourages audience members to research Cosby's legal history: 'When you leave here, Google 'Bill Cosby rape.''
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directly prompting audiences to look up information can convert a joke into a civic/educational action that spreads beyond the room; it leverages curiosity and online search to amplify impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short, memorable lines that register and repeat
rubrics_metrics.description: The routine contains concise, repeatable lines ('So, brings you down a couple notches. I don’t curse on stage. But yeah, you’re a rapist.'), which were widely quoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economy of language and punchy phrasing make a joke easy to repeat, quote, and share online — a practical requirement for virality and cultural penetration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recorded performance and online publication enabling virality
rubrics_metrics.description: Cellphone video of the performance, first featured on Philadelphia magazine's website, went viral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recording (even cellphone video) plus placement on an online platform substantially increases reach. Performers seeking social impact should consider how a routine will play on camera and online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to endure backlash and persist
rubrics_metrics.description: At the time, Buress 'got hate mail from many Cosby fans as well as praise from others,' and later said 'I got a lot of flak for that.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controversial material that challenges powerful figures often provokes strong negative responses; effective social-justice-oriented comedy requires resilience and an expectation of both support and hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with broader social context and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes that 'soon after Buress’ viral jokes, the allegations against Cosby became common knowledge' and that 'More than 60 women have spoken out.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A joke's capacity to change discourse depends on timing and the broader cultural moment; comedy that connects with ongoing concerns or unacknowledged information can catalyze public conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transforming private allegations into public conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Buress is 'credited with broadening awareness of the allegations that Bill Cosby faced' — his routine galvanized accusers and made allegations common knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective socially-conscious comedy can shift what is publicly discussable by reframing or spotlighting previously ignored claims; consider ethical responsibilities when bringing private allegations into public forums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using moral framing to undermine authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Buress targets Cosby's moralizing persona ('I can talk down to you because I had a successful sitcom') and contrasts it with alleged misconduct ('you’re a rapist').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlighting the gap between a figure's moralizing rhetoric and their conduct weakens their authority and can be a potent comedic strategy; the framing should be clear so audiences see the inconsistency.
